title: Episode 94: The Charter Oak Affair of 1687: Defying Sir Edmund Andros in the Night
description:
On October 31, 1687, royal governor Sir Edmund Andros arrived in Hartford to revoke Connecticut's sacred royal charter and absorb the colony into a centralized autocratic dominion. In a dramatic candlelit showdown, the lights were suddenly extinguished, and the charter vanished into the hollow trunk of an ancient white oak.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step back into colonial New England during the tumultuous autumn of sixteen eighty-seven, nearly a century before the American Revolution. King James the Second of England sought to crush the independent self-governance of the American colonies, appointing an authoritarian royal governor, Sir Edmund Andros, to seize their charters and unite them into a single centralized super-colony: the Dominion of New England. But when Andros marched into Hartford with an armed royal guard to seize Connecticut's parchment charter from the council table, the lamps were suddenly blown out, and the instrument of colonial liberty vanished into the night, spirited away into the hollow heart of a majestic ancient white oak. Here is George with the legendary tale of the Charter Oak.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GOLDEN CHARTER OF 1662
To understand why Connecticut colonists were willing to risk treason and execution to protect a piece of parchment, one must understand the extraordinary nature of Connecticut's Royal Charter of sixteen sixty-two. In the seventeenth century, while most American colonies operated under direct royal proprietors or royal governors appointed by the Crown, Connecticut enjoyed an unprecedented degree of democratic self-rule. Settled in the sixteen thirties by Puritan pioneers who established the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut—widely regarded as the world's first written constitution creating a government—the colony operated virtually as an independent republic in all but name.
Following the restoration of the English monarchy in sixteen sixty, Connecticut's brilliant, diplomat-governor John Winthrop the Younger traveled to London to secure formal royal recognition from the newly crowned King Charles the Second. Through charm, alchemical knowledge, and personal connections at court, Winthrop accomplished an astonishing political coup: he persuaded the king to grant Connecticut a royal charter of unparalleled liberality. Dated May tenth, sixteen sixty-two, the parchment bore the great seal of England, granting Connecticut colonists the absolute right to elect their own governor, council, and magistrates, enact their own laws, and hold clear title to their lands without royal interference.
For twenty-five years, the Golden Charter was the holy grail of Connecticut liberty. It granted the colony territorial boundaries extending from Narragansett Bay all the way west to the 'South Sea'—the Pacific Ocean. To the farmers, merchants, and ministers of the Connecticut River Valley, this royal parchment was not merely a legal instrument; it was a sacred covenant that shielded their religious autonomy, their elected institutions, and their hard-won farms from royal tyranny.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE IRON FIST OF THE DOMINION OF NEW ENGLAND
The golden age of colonial autonomy came to an abrupt, threatening halt in sixteen eighty-five with the death of King Charles the Second and the ascension of his brother, King James the Second. James was an absolute monarchist who viewed the independent, semi-republican colonies of New England with deep suspicion and open hostility. He viewed their self-governing town meetings, smuggled trade, and Puritan religious autonomy as dangerous hotbeds of sedition. The king resolved to consolidate Massachusetts, Plymouth, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, and the Jerseys into a single, centralized mega-colony governed from Boston: the Dominion of New England.
To govern this autocratic dominion with an iron fist, James appointed Sir Edmund Andros, a haughty, aristocratic former British army officer who had previously served as governor of New York. Andros possessed no patience for democratic assemblies, town meetings, or colonial traditions. Arriving in Boston in late sixteen eighty-six with a company of British redcoats, Andros immediately abolished colonial legislatures, suspended freedom of the press, imposed taxes by executive decree without representative consent, and decreed that all colonial land deeds were null and void until landowners paid exorbitant renewal fees directly to the Crown.
One by one, the colonies submitted to Andros's autocratic rule. Massachusetts saw its charter revoked; Rhode Island acquiesced under duress. But proud, stubborn Connecticut refused to surrender. For months, Governor Robert Treat and the Connecticut General Assembly engaged in a masterful campaign of diplomatic stalling, penning humble letters of loyalty to London while carefully ignoring Andros's imperious demands to turn over their sacred sixteen sixty-two charter.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ROYAL MARCH ON HARTFORD
By the autumn of sixteen eighty-seven, Sir Edmund Andros's patience was completely exhausted. Frustrated by Connecticut's insolent evasions, Andros resolved to march on Hartford in person with overwhelming military force, seize the stubborn charter by royal prerogative, and formally annex the colony into his dominion. On October twenty-sixth, Andros set out from Boston at the head of a formidable royal expedition comprising seventy-five mounted redcoats, aristocratic aides-de-camp, and royal trumpeters, their red uniforms and polished armor gleaming through the colorful New England autumn foliage.
On Monday afternoon, October thirty-first, sixteen eighty-seven, the royal procession reached the banks of the Connecticut River at Wethersfield, crossing by ferry into Hartford. The town was alive with tension. To avoid provoking open rebellion, Connecticut's seventy-five-year-old governor, Robert Treat, and the magistrates of the colony rode out to greet Andros with formal protocol, escorting the royal governor into the center of Hartford with an honor guard of the county militia. Yet beneath the courteous bows and polished speeches, an atmosphere of simmering defiance hung heavy in the air.
The two delegations convened at dusk inside the meeting house and tavern of Sanford's Inn, near the center of town. A roaring fire burned in the hearth, and tallow candles flickered in brass sconces across the long oak council table. Around the table sat Sir Edmund Andros and his armed British officers, facing Governor Robert Treat, Secretary John Allyn, and the stern, stone-faced magistrates of the Connecticut General Court.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CANDLELIT CONFRONTATION
Sir Edmund Andros took his seat with autocratic pomp and opened the proceedings by reading his royal commission from King James the Second, which formally dissolved the government of Connecticut and annexed its territory into the Dominion of New England. He then demanded that Governor Treat immediately produce the sixteen sixty-two Royal Charter, surrender the document into his custody, and step down as the chief magistrate of an illegal republic.
In response, the venerable Governor Treat rose to speak. Rather than refusing outright, Treat launched into a long, eloquent, and deliberately filibustering oration. He recounted the immense sacrifices of Connecticut's founding generation: how they had braved the Atlantic crossing, felled the primeval forest, fought bloody frontier wars against native tribes, and carved a civilized Christian commonwealth out of the wilderness with their bare hands. He spoke with tears in his eyes of how they had secured their charter from King Charles, arguing that surrendering it now felt like surrendering life itself.
For hours, Treat's solemn voice filled the room, while Secretary Allyn brought out the two prized parchment copies of the charter and placed them flat upon the table under the glowing candles. The hours dragged past eight o'clock, past nine o'clock, and into the late autumn night. Andros grew increasingly agitated, drumming his fingers upon the armrest of his chair and repeatedly cutting off Treat's philosophical appeals, insisting that the King's royal will was absolute and brook no further delay.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: DARKNESS AND THE GREAT VANISHING
Just as Sir Edmund Andros reached across the table to lay his hands upon the sacred parchment charters, the tavern fell victim to a sudden, dramatic intervention. Without warning, a sharp gust of autumn wind swept through an unlatched shutter—or, as colonial tradition insists, conspirators strategically extinguished every candle in the room simultaneously. In a split second, the meeting room was plunged into pitch-black, suffocating darkness.
Instantly, confusion erupted inside the tavern. British redcoats reached for the hilts of their broadswords, shouting for order, while colonial magistrates collided with chairs in the darkness. Shouts for tinderboxes and candles echoed through the tavern. Yet despite the sudden commotion, there was no violence, no sword drawn in anger, and not a single drop of blood spilled. For several frantic minutes, the room remained shrouded in total darkness while innkeeper Sanford scrambled to strike a spark and reignite the tallow tapers.
When the candles were finally relit and the warm glow illuminated the table, Sir Edmund Andros looked down in stunned disbelief. The council table was completely bare. The sacred parchment charters had vanished without a trace, spirited away into the black night right from under the royal governor's nose. In the shadows of the doorway, a young, daring Hartford militia captain and assemblyman named Joseph Wadsworth was already slipping quietly through the back alleys of the town, clutching the cold, rolled parchment against his chest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE HOLLOW HEART OF THE WHITE OAK
Through the darkened, autumn-chilled streets of Hartford, Captain Joseph Wadsworth sprinted with his historic prize, knowing that if British redcoats caught him with the charter, the penalty would be a traitor's noose. He made his way to Wyllys Hill, the sprawling estate of the prominent Wyllys family, which overlooked the town meadows. Standing proudly on the northern slope of the property was a colossal, ancient white oak tree—Quercus alba—known to the local Indigenous Saukiog people for centuries as a sacred landmark where council meetings were held and peace treaties concluded.
The magnificent tree was estimated to be nearly a millennium old, boasting a trunk over thirty-three feet in circumference, with massive gnarled limbs spreading over eighty feet across the lawn. At the base of the ancient trunk was a deep, natural hollow aperture, sheltered from rain and hidden beneath thick folds of furrowed bark. Reaching deep inside the hollow heart of the oak, Wadsworth carefully deposited the precious parchment charter, burying it safely in the dry cavity where no British search party would ever think to look.
Back at the tavern, Sir Edmund Andros was beside himself with fury, but he was powerless to locate the document. Unable to physically seize the charter, Andros nonetheless declared the government of Connecticut dissolved by decree, assuming the reins of administration and writing the word 'Finis' at the bottom of the General Court's official minute book. Yet without the physical charter in his hands, Andros had won only an empty bureaucratic victory. The soul of Connecticut remained hidden inside the ancient oak.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GLORIOUS REVOLUTION AND THE CHARTER'S RETURN
Sir Edmund Andros's tyrannical dominion was destined to be short-lived. In November sixteen eighty-eight, across the Atlantic in England, the Glorious Revolution erupted. The despotic King James the Second was overthrown and fled to France, replaced on the throne by William of Orange and Queen Mary. The moment news of the King's fall reached Boston in April sixteen eighty-nine, furious Massachusetts colonists staged an armed uprising, arresting Andros, throwing him into prison in irons, and shipping him back to England in disgrace.
In Hartford, the celebration was ecstatic. Governor Robert Treat and the magistrates immediately reassembled the General Assembly, triumphantly erasing Andros's 'Finis' from their records. Captain Joseph Wadsworth walked up Wyllys Hill, reached into the hollow heart of the ancient oak, and retrieved the sixteen sixty-two Royal Charter in pristine, undamaged condition. Connecticut resumed its democratic government under the very charter that had been hidden in the tree, continuing to operate under its liberal provisions until eighteen eighteen—well after the American Revolution—when it served as the direct structural model for Connecticut's state constitution.
The ancient white oak became the most sacred natural monument in Connecticut, revered nationwide as the 'Charter Oak.' It stood proudly on Wyllys Hill until August twenty-first, eighteen fifty-six, when a ferocious midnight windstorm finally felled the ancient giant at an estimated age of nearly one thousand years. The entire city of Hartford went into mourning; bells tolled from church steeples for hours, and Colt's Armory band played solemn dirges over the fallen trunk. Wood from the fallen tree was carved into historic chairs, walking sticks, and the desk of the Governor of Connecticut.
Today, Connecticut proudly bears the official moniker 'The Constitution State,' and the image of the majestic Charter Oak is emblazoned across the Connecticut state quarter. It stands as an eternal symbol of American defiance, reminding generations of citizens that the sacred flame of human liberty cannot be extinguished by imperial decrees so long as brave individuals are willing to stand together in the dark.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Charter Oak Affair established Connecticut's proud tradition of constitutional liberty, showing that the flame of freedom cannot be extinguished by royal decrees. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we step into a New Haven courtroom for the historic Amistad rebellion trial.
